brief.head: Gujarati v Bengali
brief.text: Families that take to equities compound wealth across generations, Ajay Shah said, citing US papers. He called it a major factor in the rising gulf between Gujarati and Bengali wealth. {110-C04}

brief.head: No equity, no plan
brief.text: Someone doing spreadsheet calculations told Shah that without the equity premium, the numbers cannot square for any normal affluent person, who will be miserable in old age. {110-S03}

brief.head: Her own password
brief.text: Every woman, Shah said, should know her savings rate, what an index fund is, who her service provider is and the password to her own account. {110-C10}

brief.head: Two $500 bills
brief.text: Firms are ignoring two pools of talent, Shah said: women with children who want flexibility, and older people who no longer want to show up at 9 a.m. {110-C11}

brief.head: Finance as hygiene
brief.text: Personal finance is hygiene, like health, Shah said: pay the one-time cost of learning the basics, and then about fifteen minutes a month is enough. {110-C09}

thought.text: Really no one retires till they die.
thought.who: Amit Varma, arguing that everyone has something others value, at any age

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on money for a very long life
lead.head: Retire the question
body: A friend of Amit Varma’s asked him to put one question to Ajay Shah: how much wealth do you need to retire? Varma calls Shah a picture of calm. Yet each time he asked, he said, “violence resulted.”

After a third refusal, Shah gave in. In Varma’s telling, he agreed to a whole episode “because it is a stupid question, but it is an important question because people have it on their minds”. {110-S01}
Shah’s answer was that there is no good answer. People who pin their sense of safety on a number, and reach it, he said, “are setting themselves up for grief”. What they need is a process.
## A very long life

The trouble starts with longevity. Hunter-gatherers lived thirty or forty years; in the age of agriculture you died by fifty or sixty. A healthy, affluent person today, Shah said, faces “an unbelievable life span problem”.
He pointed to Nomsita, a 21-year-old on the crew. Imagining her as an active little old lady paragliding at 121, he said, is “not at all a radical proposition”.
Traditional culture, with children nearby to care for the old, was built for medium lifespans. It is, Shah said, ill-suited to this world.

Yet long horizons also give compounding more potency. If equities deliver a real doubling every ten years, he said, that is 4x in twenty years, 8x in thirty, 16x in forty and 32x in fifty. That, he said, is the counterpoint to the longevity problem. {110-C02}
## The basic catechism

The recipe is short: save a lot, buy diversified equity index funds rather than individual shares, and spread the money across the world. Shah’s rule is to take the top 20 democracies on the Freedom House list and put about 5 per cent in each.

That roughly doubles the risk-adjusted return compared with staying in India alone. Diversifying all over the world, he said, is “a free lunch. Why would anybody ever be stuck in one country?” {110-C03}

What the recipe will not give you is a number. Shah listed three strikes against the retirement spreadsheet: you cannot know your returns, you cannot know the cost of what you will consume, and you cannot know yourself.
“There is one most important thing which you don’t know anything about, which is you, which is your heart,” he said. {110-C05}
The yearning for a locked-down plan, he argued, comes from insecurity. Better to do the hygiene, accept radical uncertainty and “deal with the future as it comes”.
## Nobody really retires
Even the word retirement, Shah said, comes from an industrial age in which you stopped work at fifty-five and died by sixty. People who drop into true retirement suffer a rapid collapse in health.
If you hate your life, he said, the answer is to reinvent it, not idleness. Change course, by all means, but stay engaged with work and with people.
Part of the job belongs to the state: steady 4 per cent inflation, no fiscal crisis, law and order, working markets, and no capital controls, which Shah called immoral.
The prize, he said, is that an ordinary person should be able to buy an index fund and forget about it. {110-C12}
Varma closed with advice of his own: invest in great music. The Led Zeppelin CD beside Shah may be worthless now, he said, “but the music remains with you”.

second.label: China’s missing premium
second.head: A miracle with a hole
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a fast-growing economy whose stock market never paid its people
body: China grew fast, yet it is singular, Ajay Shah said, in being a country where equity index performance never happened. Perhaps the GDP data is a bit fake; perhaps the government grabbed whatever wealth was created. {#fakegdp} He thinks both have been happening.

Capital controls then trapped people’s money at home. Unable to plan for long lives, households piled into property. “Everybody in China idiotically buys real estate,” Shah said, and many houses will never be used. {#realestate}
He called it the hole in the heart of the China model: a success for the state, not for its people. His plea was to “look at it from the viewpoint of the people, not the state”. {110-C14}

quote.text: We create a country for the benefits of the people, not for the arrogance and the pride of the state personnel.

second.caption: China’s missing equity premium

third.head: Cheap phones, dear doctors
body: Anything machines can make will crash in price, Ajay Shah said. He had paid ₹20,000 for his phone; its level of capability will assuredly cost ₹1,000. {#phone}

Anything that needs people will keep getting dearer, because GDP growth pushes wages up. Listing cooks and drivers, he caught himself: “oops, driverless cars. Scratch that.” Personal services, he said, “will go to infinity”. {110-C06}
The economist William Baumol figured this out, Shah said: a doctor’s consultation will cost ever more steel as steel gets cheaper to make.

His point was not that old age will be dear. “I’m not here to take a stand on the idea that your life will become very expensive,” he said. {#dontknow} “I am here to take a stand on the idea that we don’t know.”
third.caption: Baumol’s cost disease

p2.title: Forget the number
p2.deck: Why Ajay Shah calls the retirement number the wrong question, and what he would do instead {110-S01}

sections.label: The question
sections.head: An operating system for 121
sections.caption: why there is no good answer
body: Ajay Shah began by rejecting the question. There is no good answer to how much wealth you need to retire, he said, and if you fall in love with an answer, beware of getting what you wish. What we need is “the wisdom of accepting uncertainty about the world”.

The deeper problem is longevity. In the hunter-gatherer age, he said, you grew up and rapidly died; in the age of agriculture you were gone by fifty or sixty. Young Nomsita, all of twenty-one, must now plan for 121. {110-J03}
## Built for shorter lives

Traditional culture was designed for medium lifespans, with children nearby to care for parents in old age. Now the family is in decline: people have fewer children and spend less time with family. That raises the question of what it means to grow old. {110-C01}

Amit Varma added a problem of mindset. People treat life as a destination, he said, where you reach a sum of money, retire and sail off into the sunset. But life is a continuous process. His own biggest fear is living longer, with more of it lost to dementia. {#dementia}
~ The framing may be faulty, Varma conceded, but the worry is valid: what must I do financially so that I don’t run into trouble as I go along?

quote.text: So our traditional operating system is ill suited for this world.

sections.label: The counterweight
sections.head: Paid to wait, not to gamble
sections.caption: the equity premium
body: The heart of good financial planning, Ajay Shah said, is equity investment, and “the magic phrase is the equity premium”: the higher average return earned for holding diversified equities. The universe does not pay you for foolish, undiversified risk, only for the systematic risk left after diversifying.

Long lives make it stronger. With a real doubling every ten years, he said, wealth grows 32 times in fifty, and over long decades the ups and downs tend to cancel out. The equity premium is the counterpoint to the longevity problem. {110-C02}
Small changes in the expected return get magnified over such horizons, so the size of the premium matters. “You can’t be philosophical about it,” he said.
## From one country to twenty

Diversification runs from one company to many, from one industry to twenty and, the biggie, from one country to many. The United States has bad decades and Japan good ones; on average it cancels out. Holding twenty countries, Shah said, roughly doubles the risk-adjusted return of any one alone. {110-C03}
~ The fewer years you have, the more it matters. With sixty years, a 40 per cent drawdown in India alone can be ridden out. With twenty or thirty, the answer is international diversification.

quote.text: So in a way, the counterpoint to the longevity problem is the equity premium problem.

sections.label: Three strikes
sections.head: Your heart isn’t in the sheet
sections.caption: the illusion of control
body: Retirement spreadsheets are everywhere on YouTube. Ajay Shah’s objection is that they pretend to know three things nobody can know.

First, returns. Nobody should take a long-run average Nifty return, “like 13% nominal in INR”, stick it in a spreadsheet and assume it will go on smoothly. {#nifty} The premium is paid precisely because things can go wrong.

Second, what things will cost. Even the hosts’ episode *The World in 2050*, only 25 years out, sounded like science fiction, and they meant every claim, Shah said. Fifty or seventy-five years out, the world will be unimaginably different. {110-R07}

Prices will move with it. Machines will make goods ever cheaper while services that need people get dearer, a tension the economist William Baumol figured out. People will keep adjusting what they buy.
## The unknown self
Third, and most important, you: your preferences, your values, your heart. Humans, Shah said, are notoriously bad at understanding what they value. {110-C05}
Could a twenty-year-old Amit Varma have described a good life at fifty-two? He could not, Varma said: there were too many unknown unknowns.

~ The craving for a locked-down number, Shah argued, comes from insecurity. Whoever calculates X money, gets it and sets off to travel the world will be unhappy when the world changes on them. {110-C07}

quote.text: We want certainty because we are weak and we are scared.

sections.label: What to do
sections.head: Idleness is not the answer
sections.caption: getting out of the word retirement
body: Asked for actionables, Ajay Shah began with a word to drop. Retirement, he said, is an industrial-age idea: you retired at fifty-five and died by sixty. {#retire55}

In the hard data, people who go into true retirement suffer a rapid collapse in health; those who stay engaged with work and with people do better. Change course, by all means, and go live in a village in Himachal Pradesh. But keep doing stuff “with every last drop”. {110-C08}
Amit Varma had seen it: of two people retiring at the same age, the one who volunteers at a dog shelter or gives tuitions stays healthier and happier.
## A simple drill
The financial process is short: a high savings rate, and the index funds of the top 20 democracies on the Freedom House Index. {110-R04}

What of people, women especially, with no bandwidth? Shah said nobody needs to pick stocks, and operating the accounts is easy now. “It is like 3x harder to use Zerodha than it is to use Zepto.” {110-J05}

~ His suggestion for a higher savings rate was to cut spending on restaurants and alcohol. Varma protested that Swiggy survives in India because of him. Shah prescribed boiled vegetables. “Very sad,” said Varma. {110-J06}

quote.text: If you hate your life, the answer is not idleness. If you hate your life, the answer is to reinvent your life.

sections.label: Many countries
sections.head: A Magna Carta for savers
sections.caption: spreading money across the world
body: To fix intuition, Ajay Shah walked through the experiences of several countries. In the United States and the UK, the basic recipe has worked over two or three hundred years, through two world wars and a cold war.
The one dark spell was capital controls, which he said originated with Hitler in 1933 and were gone from all rich countries by the late seventies. {#hitler}
It is your money, he said, not the government’s to direct, and he called the freedom to use it as you like a Magna Carta right. {110-J13}
## Three countries, three fates

Japan’s market failed for some twenty years after its 1986 crash, but its people were free to invest abroad, and that saved them. China, Shah said, had neither working equities nor that freedom: “the worst of all worlds”.

India sits in between. Its controls, mercifully, are solvable. “You need a lawyer, you need a bank, you need an advisor, you’ll need to jump hoops,” Shah said, but it can be done and it should be done. {#lawyer}
He is proud, he said, of the Indian equity market’s progress from about 1991 to about 2009–10, the story of the hosts’ episode and his paper *The Journey of Indian Finance*. {110-R09}
~ He then made Amit Varma practise “internationalisation”, which Varma repeated until it became “intentionally internationalist”.

quote.text: It’s a Magna Carta right that it’s your money and you should use your money as you like.

sections.label: The state’s part
sections.head: Pour concrete on four per cent
sections.caption: what citizens should demand of the state
body: What should citizens demand? Ajay Shah listed five things, starting with inflation. If you have 10 per cent inflation for four years, he said, you have knocked out 50 per cent of your portfolio. {#inflation}

The issuer of the rupee should be legally accountable for 4 per cent, “not too low, not too high”, year after year. India’s inflation targeting began only on 20 February 2015, so the state must prove itself for the next ninety years. {#feb2015}
## No crisis, no gangsters
Second, no fiscal crisis. India’s debt-to-GDP ratio, he said, is about twice what it ought to be, and should be halved over the next twenty-five years.

Third, law and order, because violence is equally bad whether it comes from a gangster or a government employee. Fourth, working firms and financial markets, so that an individual can simply buy an equity index fund and forget about it. {110-C12}
Fifth, no capital controls, which Shah called immoral, as bad as refusing someone an imported dengue vaccine. {110-C13}
~ Amit Varma had a quibble with Shah’s word “societal”, and a scheme for those who distrust the state: a cryptocurrency called everything coin, run on an algorithm the hosts could not reveal. {#coin}

quote.text: It’s as bad as telling you that a certain vaccine cannot be given to you because it is imported.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah’s closing recommendation was Jeremy Siegel’s *Stocks for the Long Run*, which he called a grand book. It gives the basic intuition of two hundred years of equity index investing, and everybody, he said, should read it and internalise the message deeply. {110-R01}

contQuote.text: So that in the end, the fruit of the labour is that an individual should be able to dumbly buy an equity index fund and forget about it.

p3.title: Tales from the long run
p3.deck: Four stories from the episode, and what each says about planning a long life

stories.start: In Japan, there was a giant mess in the Japanese macro economy
stories.end: buy their index funds. That recipe would have worked in Japan
stories.caption: Japan’s lost decades
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a crash, two decades, and an open door
stories.head: Twenty dead years, one way out
body: To show why owning one country is not enough, Ajay Shah turned to Japan. Through the 1970s and 1980s, he said, there was “a giant mess in the Japanese macro economy”, and it led to a great crash that began in 1986.
What surprised him was what followed. For a very long time after 1986, the equity market simply did not deliver. There was a twenty-year period in which equities did badly. {#twenty}
For a saver who held on through that stretch, it was frightening. Anyone holding Japan alone, Shah said, “really got a terrible and abysmal performance” from the equity portfolio.

But Japan was an advanced democracy, and there were no capital controls. The Japanese government, he said, did not interfere with the freedom of its people. {#japanfree} A Japanese saver could spread money all over the world.
That was the rescue. “The way to protect financial planning through the very unusual catastrophe of the Japanese economy from 1986 to 2006 to 2010 was global diversification,” Shah said. {110-S04}

Recipe one, holding an equity index fund at home, would not have worked in Japan for that period. Recipe two would have: go to the Freedom House list, find the top 20 democracies of the world and buy their index funds.
~ Shah had already set Japan beside the United States and the UK, where the basic recipe worked for two or three hundred years. Japan is the case where recipe one failed for twenty years.
stories.why: Even a rich, free country’s market can fail its savers for decades. Owning the home index is recipe one; owning the indexes of many democracies is recipe two, and recipe two is what survives.
stories.postscript: Next came China, which Shah called “a really bad situation”: no equity performance, and capital controls besides. {110-R08}

stories.start: This is a profound point and the reason the twenty year old me
stories.end: What if you have hyperinflation? What happens, your savings get wiped out?
stories.caption: India’s vanished STD booths
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the future nobody could have predicted
stories.head: A million booths, then none
body: Ajay Shah asked whether a twenty-year-old Amit Varma could have described a good life at fifty-two. Varma said he could not.
At twenty, he said, he could never have imagined smartphones, or AI that turns images into video, or holding the means of production to make YouTube shows and films. {#smartphones}

His example was the telephone. “Before mobile telephony came, India had a million STD booths,” he said. “Today we have none.” Those jobs were lost, but the economy and productivity grew, and new jobs sprouted in ways nobody could have imagined. {110-S05}

~ The good surprises, he believes, come through technology, because that is what history has shown. The bad ones come from politics and geopolitics: what if there is a war, or hyperinflation, and savings get wiped out? {#war}
stories.why: The future arrives as unknown unknowns. To think it can be linearly extrapolated from today’s world, Varma said, is “just stupid”. Better to plan a process of living, so that you are always kind of okay.

stories.start: So let me commit this from The layman's perspective or from the perspective
stories.end: the danger of losing everything, which is absolutely not the case
stories.caption: money left in a savings account
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the middle-class script he once followed
stories.head: Burning money, safely
body: Twenty years ago, Amit Varma said, Ajay Shah’s personal finance module might have changed his life. He doubts he would have understood it then, or even been receptive.
He had followed the typical Indian middle-class script: get an education, have a career, put the salary in the bank, and keep it in fixed deposits or a savings account to be safe. {#script}

It took him a long time to see that this was a losing proposition. Inflation is so high, he said, that money kept in a savings account, as he kept his for the longest time, is money being burned. {110-S02}
~ The script has its fears too. The moment you say stock market, Varma said, the middle-class mind thinks of risk and of losing everything, “which is absolutely not the case”. {#stockmarket}
stories.why: The safe default can quietly destroy wealth. What you want, Varma said, is not to rely only on being able to work for a living, but to let whatever money you make work for you.

stories.start: And I came across this interesting uh bit of trivia yesterday
stories.end: first world kind of problem. I think uh Indian problems would be very different
stories.caption: Japan’s minister for loneliness
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s trivia from an ageing Japan
stories.head: Minister for lonely hearts
body: Amit Varma came across a piece of trivia the day before recording, one he felt he should have known, since he follows governments closely: Japan has had a minister for loneliness for a few years. {110-S06}

The post is mainly for old people. Japan is going through the opposite demographic transition to India’s, with tons of old people and questions of loneliness, so the minister organises scrabble and carrom tournaments to keep them occupied.
Varma called it a very first-world problem, and said Indian problems would be very different.
~ It fitted Ajay Shah’s warning that the family, the old support system for the aged, is in decline. Japan, Shah said, is already building robots to give frail old people a bath. {#bath}

quote.text: Japan now apparently, in fact for a few years, has a minister for loneliness.
